items.source_anchor: higher for deep in-the-money and deep
items.description: Foreign-currency options: implied volatility is higher for deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money strikes than at the money, a smile that is roughly symmetric about the money.
items.explanation: The curvature slider bends both wings at once. Positive curvature lifts the deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money strikes above the at-the-money level, which is the currency smile: the implied distribution is fatter than lognormal in both tails (exchange-rate volatility is far from constant and rates jump, sometimes on central-bank action), so options struck well away from the money on either side are dearer than BSM says. The starting curve has the opposite polarity, the frown, which the notes tie to a single anticipated price jump instead.

items.source_anchor: options. There is essentially an inverse relationship between implied volatility and
items.description: Equity options: implied volatility is highest for low-strike options and falls as the strike rises, a skew or smirk that never turns back up.
items.explanation: The tilt slider decides which wing is dear. A negative tilt puts the highest implied volatility at low strikes, the inverse relationship between implied volatility and X/S0 that the notes call a skew or smirk. The implied equity distribution has a heavier left tail and a thinner right tail than lognormal; the two explanations offered are leverage (a falling share price raises leverage and so volatility) and crashophobia (deep out-of-the-money puts carry a premium as crash protection). A positive tilt would make high strikes dear, which is not the equity pattern.

items.source_anchor: Frown:} at-the-money implied volatility is the
items.description: A single anticipated price jump turns the curve upside down: at-the-money options carry the highest implied volatility, and in-the-money and out-of-the-money options are lower. This is the frown.
items.explanation: Negative curvature puts the peak at the money. An anticipated jump makes the distribution of price changes bimodal, with the same mean and standard deviation, moving probability away from the centre toward two specific outcomes rather than into the tails, so at-the-money options become the expensive ones. Positive curvature gives the smile instead, which comes from fat tails in both directions: the notes present the two as a polarity pair.

items.source_anchor: volatilities are low from a historical perspective, volatility is an increasing function of
items.description: When short-dated implied volatilities are low from a historical perspective, at-the-money implied volatility is an increasing function of time to expiration, rising toward the long-run level.

params.name: d
params.label: Short-dated volatility minus the long-run level

params.name: k
params.label: Speed of convergence toward the long-run level

items.explanation: The gap between short-dated volatility and the long-run level sets the direction. With the short end below the long-run level, the term structure climbs toward it as maturity lengthens, so volatility is an increasing function of maturity. A short end above the long-run level produces the inverse function instead. Both cases converge toward the same long-run level, which the notes relate to (but distinguish from) the mean-reverting behaviour of implied volatility.

items.source_anchor: maturity; when they are high, it is an inverse function
items.description: When short-dated implied volatilities are high from a historical perspective, at-the-money implied volatility is an inverse function of time to expiration, falling toward the long-run level.

params.name: d
params.label: Short-dated volatility minus the long-run level

params.name: k
params.label: Speed of convergence toward the long-run level

items.explanation: A short end above the long-run level makes the term structure fall as maturity lengthens: volatility is an inverse function of maturity. Put the short end below the long-run level and the curve rises instead. Either way it converges toward the same long-run level.

items.source_anchor: options tend to exhibit \textbf{less} of a volatility smile pattern than
items.description: Long-dated options exhibit much less of a volatility smile than short-dated ones: the smile is still there, but its curvature has flattened.
items.explanation: Curvature is the slider that separates a one-month smile from a two-year smile. Reading across the volatility surface, each maturity is a smile and the curvature flattens as maturity lengthens, which is the same fact as "long-dated options exhibit less of a smile". The starting curvature is the steep short-dated smile.

items.source_anchor: Heavier left tail \textit{and} heavier right tail
items.description: The implied distribution of an exchange rate is fatter than the lognormal in both tails: extreme moves in either direction are more likely than BSM assumes.
items.explanation: The weight on the wide component is what puts extra mass in both tails. With it at zero the curve is a single bell with thin tails; with it switched on, both tails are heavier, so options struck well below and well above the money are dearer than BSM says and implied volatility rises at both ends. That is why currencies show a smile. The notes attribute the fat tails to non-constant volatility and to jumps in exchange rates.

items.source_anchor: Heavier left tail, thinner right tail
items.description: The implied distribution of an equity price is fatter than the lognormal in the left tail only and thinner in the right: large down moves are more likely than large up moves.

params.name: w
params.label: Weight of the extra tail mass

params.name: m
params.label: Location of the extra tail mass

items.explanation: Where the extra tail mass sits decides the smile shape. Put it on the left (large falls) and only low-strike options are dear, so implied volatility falls monotonically with strike: the equity skew. Moving it to the right would make large rises the likely extreme, the opposite of what equity traders believe relative to the lognormal.

items.source_anchor: The expected rate never reaches $\theta$; it approaches it asymptotically
items.description: Under the Vasicek model the expected short rate is pulled toward its long-run level and approaches it asymptotically: the gap closes quickly at first and ever more slowly after, never quite reaching it.
items.explanation: The speed of mean reversion k is the rate at which the gap between the current rate and theta decays: E[r_T] = theta - (theta - r0)e^(-kT), with half-life ln(2)/k. With the notes' example (r0 6.2%, theta 18%, k 0.03) the expected rate is 9.26% after ten years and about 12.1% at the 23.1-year half-life. At k = 0 the pull disappears and the expected path is flat forever, which is Model 1 (no drift).

items.source_anchor: Flat volatility term structure:} it predicts a flat term structure of volatility
items.description: The no-drift model, with a constant volatility, predicts a flat term structure of volatility, in contrast to the hump-shaped pattern that is observed.
items.explanation: With no decay and no build-up, every term carries the same volatility: the flat volatility term structure the notes list as a Model 1 weakness (observed volatility is hump-shaped). A positive decay is what a mean-reverting model such as Vasicek adds, and it tilts the curve down.

items.source_anchor: declining volatility is produced, where short-term
items.description: The Vasicek model produces a declining term structure of volatility: short-term volatility is relatively high and long-term volatility comparatively low.
items.explanation: The decay term is mean reversion showing up in volatility: shocks to the short rate dissipate as rates revert to the long-run mean, so short-term rates are affected more than long-term rates. The notes add that this overstates short-term and understates long-term volatility. With zero decay the curve is flat, which is the no-drift Model 1 result.

items.source_anchor: Term structure of interest rates:} downward sloping, and rates can go negative
items.description: The no-drift model produces a downward-sloping term structure of interest rates: longer maturities carry lower rates.
items.explanation: The short-minus-long spread sets the slope of the whole curve. A positive spread puts short maturities above long ones, the downward-sloping term structure the notes attribute to Model 1's no-drift assumption. A negative spread would give the upward-sloping curve that Model 2's positive drift produces.

items.source_anchor: Empirical and implied volatility curves hump: low at the very short end, peaking at intermediate
items.description: Gauss+ can be calibrated to the hump-shaped volatility term structure seen in markets: low short-term volatility, higher medium-term volatility, declining long-term volatility.
items.explanation: The build-up term lets volatility rise with term before the decay takes over, giving a peak at intermediate terms. Set it to zero and the curve is the Vasicek shape, highest at the short end and declining. Gauss+ can produce the hump because its short-rate equation has no volatility term of its own: the short rate only drifts toward the medium-term factor, reflecting a central bank pegging the policy rate, which keeps short-end volatility low.

items.source_anchor: CIR bends
items.description: Under CIR, basis-point volatility rises with the level of the short-term rate, but it bends over: it grows with the square root of the rate, so each further rise in the rate adds less volatility.

y.label: Basis-point volatility (indexed to one at a ten per cent rate)

params.name: c
params.label: Component independent of the rate level

params.name: s
params.label: Component that scales with the rate level

items.explanation: The power on the rate level is the difference between the two non-negative-rate models. CIR sets basis-point volatility to sigma times the square root of r, a power of one half, so the curve rises but bends over (non-linear). A power of one is the lognormal model, whose volatility rises in a straight line through the origin.

items.source_anchor: straight line through the origin, so at zero rates it gives zero volatility
items.description: In the lognormal model, yield volatility is constant, so basis-point volatility rises in a straight line through the origin as the rate level rises: at zero rates it gives zero volatility.

y.label: Basis-point volatility (indexed to one at a ten per cent rate)

params.name: c
params.label: Component independent of the rate level

params.name: s
params.label: Component that scales with the rate level

items.explanation: Basis-point volatility in the lognormal model is sigma times r, proportional to the rate, so the power on the rate level is one and the line is straight. A power of one half is CIR, which bends over because the square root grows more slowly than the rate.

items.source_anchor: normal model gives the same basis point volatility whether rates are at
items.description: A normal model gives the same basis-point volatility whatever the level of rates: the curve does not respond to the rate at all.

y.label: Basis-point volatility (indexed to one at a ten per cent rate)

params.name: c
params.label: Component independent of the rate level

params.name: s
params.label: Component that scales with the rate level

items.explanation: In a normal (Gaussian) model sigma is a constant number of basis points, independent of the rate level, so the component that scales with the rate must be zero. Turning it on makes volatility rise with the rate, which is the feature CIR and the lognormal model add.

items.source_anchor: Upward-sloping, because expected future rates exceed the current rate.
items.description: Under pure expectations, the spot-rate curve slopes upward when the market expects future one-year rates to exceed the current one-year rate.

params.name: e2
params.label: Expected one-year rate one year from now

params.name: e3
params.label: Expected one-year rate two years from now

items.explanation: Each spot rate is the geometric average of the current and expected one-year rates, so the shape is set solely by expected future rates. With 8%, then 10% and 12% expected, the two- and three-year spot rates are 8.995% and 9.988%: upward sloping. An expected one-year rate below the current rate for the second year pulls the two-year spot rate down and breaks the upward slope.

items.source_anchor: Downward-sloping, because expected future rates are lower than the current rate.
items.description: Under pure expectations, the spot-rate curve slopes downward when the market expects future one-year rates to fall below the current one-year rate.

params.name: e2
params.label: Expected one-year rate one year from now

params.name: e3
params.label: Expected one-year rate two years from now

items.explanation: With 8% today and 6% then 4% expected, the two- and three-year spot rates are 6.995% and 5.987%, so the curve slopes down. The third-year expectation drives the three-year spot rate: expecting a rebound in that year lifts the three-year rate back above the two-year rate and the curve is no longer downward sloping.

items.source_anchor: Yield curve is flat; investors are willing to lock in rates for two or three
items.description: Under pure expectations, the spot-rate curve is flat when the market expects future one-year rates to stay at the current one-year rate.

params.name: e2
params.label: Expected one-year rate one year from now

params.name: e3
params.label: Expected one-year rate two years from now

items.explanation: If the one-year rate is expected to stay at 8% for the next two years, every spot rate averages the same 8% and the curve is flat: investors are willing to lock in rates for two or three years at 8%. Expecting a higher rate in the second year bends the curve.

items.source_anchor: gap every period and approaches the mean asymptotically without ever quite arriving
items.description: A mean-reverting variable is pulled toward its long-run mean, closing a fixed share of the remaining gap every period, so it approaches the mean asymptotically without ever quite arriving.
items.explanation: The mean reversion rate a is the share of the gap S - mu closed each period: S_t - S_(t-1) = a(mu - S_(t-1)). At a = 0 there is no pull at all and the variable never moves; at a = 1 it jumps straight to the mean; at a = 0.5 it halves the remaining gap every period (50, 65, 72.5, 76.25, ...). In regression terms a is the slope with its sign flipped.

items.source_anchor: PC2 pushes short rates down while long rates rise
items.description: The second principal component of swap rates is the slope factor: it pushes short rates down while long rates rise.

y.label: Loading: basis points per one standard deviation move

items.explanation: The dip parameter is what drags the short and middle of the curve below zero while the long end stays positive, so a one-standard-deviation move in PC2 lowers short rates and raises long rates: a change in slope. Without the dip every term loads positively, which is the level factor (PC1), not the slope factor. The loadings follow the GARP data set drawn in the notes (about -1.2 bp near four years, +1.35 bp at thirty).

items.source_anchor: small and changes sign twice across the curve
items.description: The third principal component is small and changes sign twice across the curve: short and long terms move one way, the middle the other. This is the curvature factor.

y.label: Loading: basis points per one standard deviation move

items.explanation: The short-end hump gives the positive loading at the front of the curve (about +0.47 bp at two years in the notes' data); the middle turns negative and the long end positive again, so the sign changes twice. Without the hump the loading is a straight line that changes sign only once, which would be a slope-type factor, not curvature.

items.source_anchor: power, so extreme values remain possible far out
items.description: When the tail index is positive (Frechet), the tail is heavy: it decays as a power, so extreme values remain possible far out.
items.explanation: The tail index xi is the shape of the tail. A positive xi gives the Frechet case with power-law decay, the one to use for financial losses (t and Pareto parents, and the conservative choice because the estimated risk measure increases with the tail index). A negative xi is the Weibull case, which has a finite upper bound and simply stops, so it is no use for losses. xi = 0 (Gumbel) decays exponentially and is not on this slider, because the formula changes form there.

items.source_anchor: the distribution has a finite upper bound and simply stops
items.description: When the tail index is negative (Weibull), the tail is lighter than a normal one and bounded: the distribution has a finite upper end-point and simply stops.
items.explanation: A negative tail index caps the support at mu - sigma/xi, so the density reaches zero and stays there. The notes say distributions with xi < 0 rarely appear in financial models for exactly this reason. A positive xi instead leaves a power-law tail that is still alive far out.

items.source_anchor: Fat-tailed: they separate
items.description: A fat-tailed loss distribution: the same tail region contains far larger losses than under a normal distribution, so expected shortfall is pulled well beyond VaR.

params.name: w
params.label: Weight of the wide tail component

items.explanation: The wide component is what makes the tails heavy. With it at zero the curve is normal: the tail is thin, and 97.5% ES (2.338 sigma) lands almost exactly on 99% VaR (2.326 sigma). With it switched on, the tail beyond the VaR cut holds much larger losses and ES is pulled well beyond VaR, which the notes call the whole argument for the switch from VaR to ES.

items.source_anchor: and the curve is concave, so the risk
items.description: For two long positions, VaR rises as the correlation between them rises, and the curve is concave, so the risk reduction accelerates as correlation falls.

x.label: Correlation between asset one and asset two

params.name: a
params.label: Position one: amount times daily volatility

params.name: b
params.label: Position two: amount times daily volatility

params.name: z
params.label: Normal deviate times square root of the horizon

items.explanation: Correlation enters VaR only through the cross term 2 rho a b, so it needs two positions to act on. With the notes' example (USD 10m at 2% and USD 5m at 1% daily volatility, 99%, ten days) VaR runs from about USD 1.10m at rho = -1 to about 1.84m at rho = +1, and is USD 1.75m at the worked rho = 0.7. The square root makes the curve concave. With the second position at zero, correlation has nothing to act on and VaR is flat.

items.source_anchor: Capital gains are \term{capped} by the call price.
items.description: A callable bond's price-yield curve flattens as yields fall: price gains are capped by the call price, which is what negative convexity looks like.

params.name: k
params.label: Option-free price curve: sensitivity to yield

items.explanation: The call price is the ceiling. Once yields fall far enough that the option-free price would pass it, the callable bond's price cannot rise past the call price and the curve goes flat at low yields. With the call price set above anything the option-free bond reaches, the option never binds and the curve keeps its ordinary convex shape.

items.source_anchor: The put price serves as a \term{floor} value for the bond price.
items.description: A putable bond cannot fall past the put price as yields rise: the put price is a floor, so the bond is less sensitive to yield increases at the high end.

params.name: k
params.label: Option-free price curve: sensitivity to yield

items.explanation: The put price is the floor. When yields rise far enough that the option-free price would drop below it, the putable bond's price cannot fall past the put price, so the curve goes flat at high yields. With the put price below anything the option-free bond reaches in this range, the floor never binds.

items.source_anchor: Swaps \emph{peak}, because future payment uncertainty rises while the
items.description: An interest rate swap's credit exposure profile peaks: future payment uncertainty rises over time while the number of remaining payments falls.

x.label: Time, as a share of the contract maturity

params.name: g
params.label: Build-up of exposure uncertainty with time

params.name: p
params.label: Run-off of the remaining payments by maturity

items.explanation: Two forces pull in opposite directions. Uncertainty about future rates builds with time and pushes exposure up; the payments still to be exchanged run off and pull it back toward zero at maturity. The run-off slider is the second force: at full run-off the profile peaks in the middle of the swap's life. Without run-off exposure only grows, which is the FX-product profile, not a swap's. (Illustrative shape: the notes draw these profiles without numbers.)

items.source_anchor: FX products increase monotonically, driven by
items.description: An FX product's credit exposure profile increases monotonically over the life of the trade, driven by FX volatility and a large final exchange of notional.

x.label: Time, as a share of the contract maturity

params.name: g
params.label: Build-up of exposure uncertainty with time

params.name: p
params.label: Run-off of the remaining payments by maturity

items.explanation: FX exposure is driven by FX volatility and by the large exchange of notional at the end of the trade, so it keeps rising until maturity. Adding run-off bends the profile into the peak that belongs to swaps. (Illustrative shape: the notes draw these profiles without numbers.)

items.source_anchor: correlation for very risky \emph{and} very safe tranches.
items.description: Compound (tranche) correlation, implied tranche by tranche, shows a smile: higher correlation for the very risky and the very safe tranches, lower in the middle of the capital structure.

x.label: Tranche, most junior (equity) to most senior (super senior)

items.explanation: Curvature across the capital structure produces the smile: high at the equity and super-senior ends, low in the mezzanine. Compound correlation comes out this way because each tranche is solved on its own. Base correlation, which is cumulative across the structure, rises monotonically instead and is called the skew. (Illustrative shape: the notes say no market data are used.)

items.source_anchor: where safer tranches have higher implied correlation.
items.description: Base correlation, which treats the CDO cumulatively, shows a skew: safer tranches have higher implied correlation, rising monotonically from equity to super senior.

x.label: Tranche, most junior (equity) to most senior (super senior)

items.explanation: The tilt sets the direction across the capital structure. Base correlation is adjusted so that each tranche's model present value of losses matches the market, and the result rises with seniority: the skew. A negative tilt would make the junior tranches the high-correlation ones, which is not what either measure shows. (Illustrative shape: the notes say no market data are used.)

items.source_anchor: the debtholders are capped at $F$ and every further dollar goes to equity
items.description: In the Merton model the equity payoff is a long call on the firm's assets: worth nothing while assets are below the face value of the debt, then every further dollar goes to equity.

x.label: Firm asset value at T, V_T

y.label: Value of equity at T, S_T

params.name: F
params.label: Face value of the debt, F

params.name: bL
params.label: Share of each asset dollar below F

params.name: bU
params.label: Share of each asset dollar above F

items.explanation: S_T = max(V_T - F, 0). Below F the debtholders take everything, so the slope there is zero; above F the debtholders are capped at F, so equity collects the whole of each further asset dollar and the slope is one. The kink at F is what makes the payoff convex, the shape of a long call struck at F. In the worked points, V_T = 60 gives S_T = 10 and V_T = 40 gives 0.

items.source_anchor: the debtholders take everything and the equity is worth nothing
items.description: In the Merton model the debt payoff is the face amount less a put struck at the face value, so debtholders are short that put: they take everything while assets are below the face value, and are capped at the face value above it.

x.label: Firm asset value at T, V_T

y.label: Value of debt at T, D_T

params.name: F
params.label: Face value of the debt, F

params.name: bL
params.label: Share of each asset dollar below F

params.name: bU
params.label: Share of each asset dollar above F

items.explanation: D_T = F - max(F - V_T, 0). Below F the debt takes every asset dollar (slope one); above F it is capped at F (slope zero), because every further dollar goes to equity. That cap makes the payoff concave: debtholders are short a put struck at F. Letting debt share in the upside turns the payoff into a straight line, which would leave nothing for the equity call.

items.source_anchor: gives the largest CVA, mainly because it produces the largest
items.description: An upward-sloping credit curve, pinned at the same five-year spread as the flat and inverted curves: longer maturities carry wider spreads.

params.name: b
params.label: Slope (spread change per year of maturity)

items.explanation: The slope is the only thing that differs between the three curves, since all are pinned at 150 bp at five years. An upward slope produces the largest extrapolated ten-year spread, which is why it gives the largest CVA on a ten-year swap in the notes' illustration (-24.6 against -20.0 flat and -15.7 inverted, at 60% LGD).

items.source_anchor: the inverted curve gives the smallest for the opposite reason
items.description: An inverted credit curve, pinned at the same five-year spread as the flat and upward curves: shorter maturities carry wider spreads than longer ones.

params.name: b
params.label: Slope (spread change per year of maturity)

items.explanation: A negative slope inverts the curve. Because all three curves share the five-year point, the inverted one has the smallest extrapolated ten-year spread and so gives the smallest CVA on the ten-year swap (-15.7 against -20.0 flat and -24.6 upward, at 60% LGD). The shape of the credit curve alone moves CVA 21% below and 23% above the flat case.

items.source_anchor: and can be symmetric or skewed based on its shape parameters, which determine
items.description: Credit losses are not normally distributed and tend to be highly skewed: many small loss rates and a long tail of large ones, modelled with a beta distribution on losses between none and all.
items.explanation: The beta distribution is used because it confines losses to between 0% and 100%, and its two shape parameters decide symmetry and tail behaviour. Equal parameters give a symmetric curve; making b much larger than a piles the mass at low loss rates and leaves a long right tail, the highly skewed shape the notes say credit losses take. That tail is what economic capital is set against.

items.source_anchor: which bends the line upward at the origin
items.description: A manager with market-timing ability holds more market exposure when the market beats the risk-free rate and less when it does not, so the characteristic line bends upward at the origin, like a long call.

params.name: bD
params.label: Beta when the market trails the risk-free rate

params.name: bU
params.label: Beta when the market beats the risk-free rate

items.explanation: The up-market beta is beta_P + M_P and the down-market beta is beta_P. A positive M_P, an up-market beta above the down-market beta, is the indication of timing ability and bends the line upward at the origin. Estimating M_P is estimating the size of that bend. With equal betas the line is straight and there is no timing.

items.source_anchor: is straight: one beta in all states.
items.description: With no market-timing ability the security characteristic line is straight: one beta in all states of the market.

params.name: bD
params.label: Beta when the market trails the risk-free rate

params.name: bU
params.label: Beta when the market beats the risk-free rate

items.explanation: No timing means the manager's beta does not change with the market, so the up-market and down-market betas are equal and M_P = 0. Raising the up-market beta above the down-market one would bend the line upward: that kink is the genuine skill the dummy-variable regression measures through M_P.

items.source_anchor: skewness in their return distribution, meaning a higher potential for losses on
items.description: Certain nonlinear strategies exhibit negative skewness in their return distribution: a higher potential for losses in the left tail.

params.name: sL
params.label: Spread of outcomes below the most likely return

params.name: sR
params.label: Spread of outcomes above the most likely return

items.explanation: Stretching the spread on the downside while the upside stays tight gives a long left tail: frequent small gains and occasional large losses. The notes warn that alpha calculations typically do not account for this skewness. With equal spreads the distribution is symmetric and the problem disappears.

items.source_anchor: Riding the yield curve requires an \emph{upward-sloping yield curve}
items.description: Riding the yield curve requires an upward-sloping yield curve, with longer maturities yielding more than shorter ones, not an upward-sloping price.
items.explanation: A negative short-minus-long spread puts short yields below long ones: the upward-sloping curve the strategy needs. The strategy rests on the fact that as time passes a bond's remaining maturity and duration decrease: the manager buys long-term bonds, and after the yield declines sells and rolls out the curve to repeat the process, buying another bond at the end of a steep segment of the curve. The trap the notes flag is to confuse this with an upward-sloping price.

items.source_anchor: Characterised by many minor losses and a few major ones, operational risks
items.description: Operational losses are heavy tailed: many minor losses and a few major ones, with significant asymmetry in the loss distribution.
items.explanation: The curve is a generalized Pareto shape (the excess-loss model of MR-3) used here only to draw the shape. A positive tail index leaves a long, slowly decaying right tail: most losses are minor, but large, infrequent ones such as rogue-trading incidents remain possible, which is the managing challenge the notes name. A negative tail index would cap the size of loss, which is exactly what operational risk does not do.
